[MUQATIL:89:15-22/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The passage was revealed about Umayya b. Khalaf and ʿAbd Allāh b. Nufayl: after Nufayl advised him to do good and avoid evil, Umayya cited 47:11, asked why God enriched him but impoverished Nufayl, then claimed wealth proved his honor; Ibn Khaṭal said God might indeed have done so. | mentions 47:11
[MUQATIL:89:15-22/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | Wealth does not show God's honor or poverty His contempt: God meant to give the rich man ease in this life and make the poor man's reckoning lighter in the Hereafter.
[MUQATIL:89:15-22/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The repeated promise that with hardship comes ease means every difficulty is followed by relief, and every ease by later difficulty. | mentions 94:5, 94:6
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ألقيت زيدا أو عمرا and أعندك زيد أو خالد, أو asks whether any listed person was encountered or is present; placing names after the verb is clearer when asking about the action.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · صفية بنت عبد المطلب | reports | Ṣafiyya bint ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib asks whether the object was food or a Qurashi, not which of two foods it was.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أعندك زيد أو عندك عمرو أو عندك خالد asks whether any of these states of being present obtains, like a sequence of actions.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أعاقل عمرو أو عالم and أتضرب عمرا أو تشتمه make two predicates or actions alternatives for one person, paralleling one action for one of two people.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أتضرب أو تحبس زيدا is like أزيدا أو عمرا تضرب; Jarīr illustrates it, and أزيدا تضرب أو تقتل can mean kill Zayd or ʿAmr.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r14] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In أتجلس أم تذهب and أتضرب زيدا أو تقتل خالدا, أم and أو can be equivalent because their functions cannot be separated by the pronoun marker.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r15] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | When asking which paired action applies, use أم, as in أتضرب زيدا أم تقتل خالدا.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Fronting alternatives such as أزيدا لقيت أو عمرا remains grammatical and can be natural when asking which person was involved.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أزيد أفضل أم عمرو requires أم because it asks which is better; it means أيهما, and أزيد أفضل cannot stand alone in this sense.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | ما أدري أزيد أفضل أم عمرو and ليت شعري أزيد أفضل أم عمرو likewise mean which of the two is better.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In ما أبالي أضربت زيدا أم عمرا, only أم is suitable because it asks which alternative; fronting the names is preferable.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أتجلس أو تذهب أو تحدثنا asks whether any of those actions will happen; to ask which one, use أم.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With different actions and objects, أو asks whether any alternative occurs, while أم asks which; the same distinction appears in examples with ضرب.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Ḥassān ibn Thābit uses أم in a question meaning the speaker does not mind which action occurred.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابآخرمنأبوابأو)#517/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In أزيدا أو عمرا رأيت أم بشرا, عمرا is a parenthetic filler, not a choice paired with Zayd; the question asks whether one of those two or Bashr was seen.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Diminutives تحيت، خليف and دوين show خلف، فوق and تحت are masculine; قبل and بعد form masculine قبيل and بعيد.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some treat قيل وقال as nouns and decline them; Ibn Muqbil has تقوالك من قيل وقال, another verse has قيلا وقالا, while quotations can keep the original form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r11] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | هذا عمرو can mean this is the name ʿAmr; هذا ألف can refer to a word or letter, with lexical names uninflected and letter names declinable.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r12] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Abu Jād, Hawwāz and Ḥuṭṭī behave like ʿAmr as Arabic names; foreign Kaliman, Saʿfaṣ and Qurayshiyyāt are diptotes, with Qurayshiyyāt like ʿArafāt and Aḏriʿāt.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r13] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Alif-lām makes a form definite, just as a person is not definite without the definite article.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | أين، كيف and متى are treated as masculine adverbs like ما and من; diminutive evidence shows most adverbs are masculine.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | إذ is like الحين and is answered by متى; ثم and هنا are like أين, while حيث has an answer pattern like خلف.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Yūnus says أمام is masculine for all Arabs; إذا and لدن pattern with عند, عن is illustrated by من عن يمينه, and a language of منذ is masculine like حيث.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Where gender evidence is absent, masculine is the preferred default until femininity is established.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Other non-adverb nouns include بعض، كل، أي and حسب; قط is also a noun, as shown by its use in a predicate.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | حسب is more fully declinable than قط because it takes prepositions and modifies a noun, as in مررت برجل حسبك.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | These terms take no tanwīn as names of words; as masculine personal names they decline, except feminine وراء and قدام.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابتسميتكms477الحروفبالظروفوغيرهامنالأسماء)#546/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | If ثم، أين or حيث become a person's, letter's or word's name, they change like زيد and عمرو; quotations may keep their original form.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبفيهالياءواوا)#782/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For faʿlā nouns such as الطوبى and الكوسى, medial yāʾ becomes wāw; adjective forms such as حيكى retain yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبفيهالياءواوا)#782/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The same noun–adjective distinction appears with final yāʾ: nouns شروى and تقوى have wāw, but adjectives صديا and خزيا keep yāʾ.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماتقلبفيهالياءواوا)#782/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Forms from wāw- and yāʾ-final roots retain their original weak radical; medial conversion compensates for yāʾ’s frequent incursion.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A final yāʾ absent in connected speech can be omitted at pause; retaining it is more analogical and common, since it takes no tanwīn and resembles the yāʾ of قاضي.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Labīd's verse shortens المعلى to المعل under poetic necessity, showing final alif can be dropped at pause when meter requires.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · أبو عمرو | reports | Abū ʿAmr reads ربي أكرمن and ربي أهانن with the possessive yāʾ omitted in pause.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · النابغة | reports | Al-Nābigha omits final yāʾ in مني and إني; Sībawayh reports this usage from trusted transmitters of Arab speech.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Al-Aʿshā gives further pause forms with a missing possessive yāʾ, including أن يأتين and أنكرن.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Yāʾ in هذا قاضي، هذان غلاماي and رأيت غلامي is not deleted because its preceding consonant is still and its yāʾ is vowelled, unlike pause yāʾ in هذا القاضي.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Yāʾ is retained in connected يا غلام أقبل because the preceding consonant is still and cannot signal the genitive relation.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A speaker saying هذا غلامي and إني ذاهب keeps yāʾ at pause because it resembles the vowelled accusative yāʾ; hāʾ may indicate the vowel, while connected vocative allows deletion.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Final alif normally remains at pause even when dropped in connected speech because fatḥa and alif are lighter and Arabic favors alif after an open vowel.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابمايحذفمنالأسماءمنالياءاتفيالوقفالتيلاتذهبفي#740/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Some medial vowels are reduced in فخذ and عضد but not جمل because fatḥa is lighter; final alif is otherwise dropped at pause only under poetic necessity.

ead qaddara with gemination, meaning “he made it constricted,” equivalent to qattara; both forms are correct.
[AKHFASH:v2p578/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · بعضهم | reports | Some explain qadara as having the same meaning as qattara, to constrict provision.
[AKHFASH:v2p578/r3] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | For the doubled form qaddara, al-Akhfash says God gives provision according to a measure.
[IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p527/r1] IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB, d. 276 · author | holds | Qadara ʿalayhi rizqahu means that God constricted his provision; qadara and qattara can mean the same.
[IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL:v1p233/r3] IBNQUTAYBA-MUSHKIL, d. 276 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ says qatar/qattara and qadara/qaddara are equivalent, all meaning to constrict.
[TUSTARI:89:16/r1] TUSTARI, d. 283 · author | holds | Constrained provision means God has made one's provision tight; neither wealth nor poverty proves divine honor or contempt.
[TUSTARI:89:16/r2] TUSTARI, d. 283 · فتح الموصلي | reports | Fath al-Mawsili rejoiced and wept through the night when his fasting household had neither dinner nor lamp oil, treating the deprivation as evidence of God's favor.
[TAB:89:16/r1] TAB, d. 310 · author | holds | When tested with poverty, a person’s provision is restricted and he mistakenly says God has humiliated him, ignoring sound limbs and bodily health.
[TAB:89:16/r2] TAB, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatada calls the son of Adam’s reaction to restricted provision a quick act of disbelief.
[TAB:89:16/r3] TAB, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd explains the phrase as God narrowing a person’s provision.
[TAB:89:16/r4] TAB, d. 310 · عامة قراء الأمصار | reports | Most regional readers use the light form qadara, meaning that God constricted provision; Abu Jaʿfar reads the geminated form qaddara.
[TAB:89:16/r5] TAB, d. 310 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abu Amr takes qaddara as God giving a person what suffices him; on that reading the person would not say his Lord humiliated him.
[TAB:89:16/r6] TAB, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Tabari prefers the light reading because the authoritative readers agree on it.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The person fails to thank God for the sound limbs and bodily well-being He gave him.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · قتادة | reports | Qatāda calls the person's response a swift act of disbelief.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · ابن زيد | reports | Ibn Zayd glosses the restriction of provision as making it narrow.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · عامة قراء الأمصار | reports | Most regional readers use the light form, meaning that God constricted the person's provision.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو جعفر القارئ | reports | Abū Jaʿfar reads the verb with a doubled consonant.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r6] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · أبو عمرو بن العلاء | reports | Abū ʿAmr says the doubled form means giving enough; on that reading, the person would not call it humiliation.
[TAB-FULL:v24p377/r7] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | prefers | Al-Ṭabarī prefers the light reading because the authoritative readers agree on it.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p322/r3] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | holds | The contrasting test consists in making one's provision measured or constrained, leading the person to say that God humiliated him.
[ZAJJAJ:v5p322/r4] ZAJJAJ, d. 311 · author | rejects | Kallā rejects the person's equation of worldly abundance with honor and poverty with humiliation; this is the unbeliever who denies resurrection, whereas the believer sees honor in success toward the afterlife.
[IBNABIHATIM:v10p3428#2/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · زيد | reports | Zayd glosses restricted provision as God narrowing a person's sustenance.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p370/r1] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | فقدر عليه رزقه is read with a doubled or light dāl; Ibn Khālawayh refers to arguments already explained elsewhere.
[IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA:v1p370/r2] IBNKHALAWAYH-HUJJA, d. 370 · author | reports | In أكرمن and أهانن, one reading keeps yāʾ in connected speech but drops it at pause, with an unvowelled nūn; al-Aʿshā’s verse witnesses this ending.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · ابن كثير | reports | Ibn Kathīr in the Yazīdī transmission retains yāʾ in akramanī and ahānanī in both pause and liaison.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · عاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي | reports | These readers omit yāʾ from akraman and ahānan in both liaison and pause.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · نافع | reports | Many Nāfiʿ transmitters, including Qālūn, Warsh, and others, retain yāʾ in liaison; one report has yāʾ from the people of Medina.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو عمرو | reports | Reports from Abū ʿAmr vary: he permits either form in liaison but pauses at the nūn, with some transmitters matching Nāfiʿ or the readers who omit yāʾ throughout.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو زيد | reports | Abū Zayd describes akraman and ahānan as jussive nūns with the yāʾ deleted.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Ibn Kathīr keeps yāʾ in the verb even at pause because verbs retain final yāʾ where nouns such as qāḍin and ghāzin lose it.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Even letters normally retained may be omitted in poetic rhyme and Qurʾānic endings; Sibawayh calls such endings pauses and allows deletion in complete clauses resembling a pause.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403#2/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Pause permits changes to strong consonants too, so endings that resemble added letters are also deleted, just as feminine tāʾ is commonly dropped in vocative shortening.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p405/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Weak endings derived from lām and other suffixes are deleted under jussive and in speech, showing that they can behave like extra letters; this supports deletion at verse endings.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p405/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Sibawayh’s “more analogical” means closer to the retained underlying form, while deletion remains frequent Arabic and is especially apt at pauses.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p405/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | Yāʾ deletion occurs even outside pauses, as in Q 11:105, so it is still more fitting at verse endings such as Q 89:9.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p405/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | reports | Nāfiʿ’s connected form retains yāʾ because there is no pause, while his paused form omits it; Abū ʿAmr is also reported with both this and another pattern.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p405/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · أبو علي | holds | ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī omit yāʾ in both settings, treating the verse ending as a pause that changes the word by deletion.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r1] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | holds | Verse-final cadence licenses dropping final yāʾ where ordinary speech may retain it; rhyme can conversely require adding it.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r2] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī's reversion from retaining yāʾ to deleting it in يسر is sound and follows the more common usage.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r3] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh reports deletion of final yāʾ in pause even after the definite article, as in الداع, alongside qāḍٍ; al-Fārisi prefers deletion. | mentions 2:186
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r4] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · البزي عن ابن كثير | reports | Al-Bazzī from Ibn Kathīr retains the yāʾ in أكرمني and أهانني both in connection and pause, matching his reading of يسري.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r5] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · قنبل وعاصم وابن عامر وحمزة والكسائي | reports | These readers omit yāʾ in أكرمن and أهانن in both connection and pause, like the readers who omit it in يسر at a verse ending.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r6] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · نافع | reports | One transmission from Nāfiʿ retains yāʾ in connection in أكرمني and أهانني but drops it in pause, by analogy with his transmission of يسري.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r7] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · إسماعيل عن نافع وورش عن نافع | reports | Ismāʿīl omits yāʾ in الواد while Warsh retains it in الوادي; both reflect two pause forms for nouns ending in yāʾ with the article, not verse-final deletion.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r8] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · علي بن نصر عن أبي عمرو | reports | ʿAlī ibn Naṣr reports that Abū ʿAmr stops at the nūn in أكرمن and أهانن, as in Sībawayh's report.
[FARISI-HUJJA:v6p408/r9] FARISI-HUJJA, d. 377 · author | prefers | Al-Fārisi considers Sībawayh's report of Abū ʿAmr's stopping at the nūn more reliable than the other transmissions.
[BAQILLANI:v1p232/r1] BAQILLANI, d. 403 · author | rejects | The first praise line is disconnected from what precedes it, reflecting the poet’s recurring failure to connect ideas; the trope of glory reaching above the stars is also shared and unoriginal.
